content_units: Best Laptop Match for a CS Student

For your priorities—  battery life first, Linux compatibility second, budget under $1,200 third  —the   Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 5   is the best overall fit. It offers the most dependable Linux experience of the three while still giving strong battery life, solid performance, and a student-friendly price.
Side-by-Side Laptop Comparison
Laptop   Price   Battery/Portability   Linux Fit   Student Value
Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 5     $999     57Wh, 1.41kg     Excellent       Best balance
ASUS Vivobook 15     $949     50Wh, 1.70kg   Fair to good   Best storage for the money
Acer Swift Go 14     $1,099     65Wh, 1.25kg   Good, but less predictable   Best screen and lightest design

Why the ThinkPad E14 Wins

-   Linux compatibility:   ThinkPads are consistently among the safest Windows laptops for Linux installs. Driver, suspend, keyboard, Wi‑Fi, and trackpoint/trackpad support are usually better documented and less troublesome.
-   Battery life:   The   57Wh   battery is stronger than the ASUS’s 50Wh, and the Ryzen 7 7730U is generally a very efficient chip for coding, browsing, terminals, and light IDE use.
-   Performance for CS work:   16GB RAM and 512GB SSD are enough for programming, Docker, VS Code, IntelliJ, light VMs, and coursework.
-   Portability:   At   1.41kg  , it is easy to carry daily and still feels sturdier than many consumer laptops.
-   Value:   At   $999  , it stays comfortably under budget without obvious compromises in the areas you care about most.
Student-Focused Recommendation
1) Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 5 — Best overall
- Best match for   Linux + battery + reliability
- Ryzen 7 7730U is efficient and more than fast enough for most CS workloads
- 14-inch 1920x1200 display is practical for coding
- ThinkPad keyboards are usually a real advantage for long typing sessions
2) Acer Swift Go 14 — Best lightweight alternative
- Biggest listed battery at   65Wh
- Lightest at   1.25kg
- Higher-resolution 14-inch display is nice for coding
- Main drawback: Intel H-series chip may draw more power under sustained use, and Linux support is usually not as confidence-inspiring as ThinkPad
3) ASUS Vivobook 15 — Best if storage matters most
- Lowest price and   1TB SSD
- Bigger screen may help if you dislike 14-inch laptops
- But it is the heaviest, has the smallest battery here except not by much, and ASUS consumer models are less consistently recommended for Linux-first use
Buying Context
Using only the specs you gave, I’m assuming:
- You want to run   Linux as main OS or dual boot
- Typical use includes programming, browser tabs, note-taking, Git, IDEs, and occasional containers/VMs
- Gaming and heavy GPU workloads are not a priority
